title: Breaking: First case of bird flu in pelican detected in SA
text:
The nation’s first case of a pelican infected with H5 bird flu has been confirmed by South Australian authorities.

The bird was found at Edithburgh on South Australia’s Yorke Peninsula, and is one of four other bird flu events across the state confirmed on Monday.

South Australia's environment minister Emily Bourke said a dead sea lion found near Victor Harbor had been sent for testing.

It follows yesterday’s confirmation of another sea lion being infected with the virus.

"We've had another report today of a deceased sea lion, just off of Victor Harbor, this is a case that we will now test," Ms Bourke said.

A dead dolphin found washed ashore at Port Noarlunga will be unable to be tested for bird flu, the minister said, due to decomposition of the carcass.

South Australia has now had 295 confirmed cases of H5 bird flu in animals.

title: Mas 'fulfils his destiny' to win historic Vuelta
text:
Enric Mas has finally delivered an expectant Spanish public an overall victory at the Vuelta a España, his win confirmed at the end of the final stage into Grenada on Sunday.

Mas finished safely in the peloton during the 21st and final stage of the race, won by Norway's Tobias Johannessen.

The 31-year-old from Mallorca held off four-time Vuelta champion Primož Roglič to become the first Spaniard to win the Vuelta since Alberto Contador in 2014.

Mas finished 2 minutes and 15 seconds ahead of Roglič overall, with Austria's Felix Gall finishing third at 2:44.

"It's just special," Mas told reporters after the race.

"It's been a day to remember, a special Vuelta, and it has been wonderful.

"There's always tension about what could happen, but you've seen it all went smoothly, so we're delighted and we enjoyed every kilometre today.

"It was a long wait and a long way to today. But to be honest, it was always special Vueltas, and this one I think is the special one."

Primož Roglič (left), has won four Vuelta's, while Enric Mas (centre) finally claimed his first aged 31. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

Five-time Tour de France winner Tadej Pogačar had come into the race as the overwhelming favourite for victory, building an ominous lead of 3 minutes 50 seconds by the end of the seventh stage.

The freakish Slovenian star had won three of the six completed stages at that stage and looked set to claim a win of unparalleled dominance in the modern era.

However, the two-time reigning world champion badly crashed on the eighth stage of the race, breaking his collar bone and fracturing his neck, ending his season.

From that point though, Mas, who had tested Pogačar on the mountainous fourth stage in Andorra, dominated the race alongside his much-maligned Movistar team.

Mas had finished second at his home grand tour three times, in 2018, 2021 and 2022, and also finished third in 2024.

When he finished second to Simon Yates in 2018, triumphing on the queen stage at that year's race, there was an expectation that Mas would become the heir to seven-time grand tour winner Contador as Spanish cycling's next big thing.

Mas even spent his junior years racing with the Alberto Contador Academy, indicating just how high hopes were that he would excel.

And although Mas has achieved plenty, finishing in the top six overall at grand tours eight times over the course of his career, the expected Contador-like dominance never eventuated.

It is telling that long-time AS reporter Juan Gutiérrez entitled his post-Vuelta piece: "Enric Mas cumple su destino", "Enric Mas fulfils his destiny".

Movistar switched their usual blue jerseys for red ones to honour Enric Mas's achievement. (Getty Images: Alexander Hassenstein)

Contador wrote in Spanish newspaper AS that he was "very happy and incredibly excited" to see Mas achieve his potential.

"I know how hard he's worked these past few years and how much criticism he's always faced," Contador said.

"Instead of letting it get him down, he turned it into motivation to demonstrate the talent he truly possesses.

"Every cyclist develops in their own way and, in Enric's case, it was fast because he finished second in the 2018 Vuelta a España.

"Then, when he didn't quite seal the deal, well, we all know how sports are — it seems like if you don't win, nothing has any merit.

"That's why cycling will be fair to Enric Mas for winning this Vuelta."

Contador acknowledged that Pogačar would likely had claimed victory had he remained in the race, but that Mas thoroughly deserved his victory.

" It's not a gift," Contador said. "It's thanks to his hard work and his form. He was the strongest. "

Santiago Buitrago of Colombia and Team Bahrain Victorious claimed the king of the mountains jersey, while British rider Oscar Onley won the white youth jersey.

Wout van Aert added some personal closure by claiming the green sprinter's jersey, and the super combative prize, after he crashed out while leading both the points and king of the mountains classifications in 2024.

"In a way this is finished business," van Aert said.

"After the near miss two years ago and the big injury I had afterwards, it was quite a disappointment.

"It makes it more special to be here, to come completely to the end, and to wear this beautiful jersey."

title: 'Godfather of AI' backs Anthropic chief's call to slow down development
text:
Geoffrey Hinton, widely known as the "godfather of AI", has backed calls for artificial intelligence (AI) companies to slow the pace of development.

Yesterday, Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei called on AI firms to slow development, saying rogue agents could be capable of "taking over the entire internet" within six to 12 months.

Professor Hinton, a British-Canadian cognitive psychologist and computer scientist, told ABC Radio National Breakfast that Mr Amodei's warning was "very sensible".

"Nobody knows how to estimate the probabilities of these things. [An Anthropic employee] said 10 per cent. Nobody really knows what figure to give.

"It's not 1 per cent, it's more than that, and it's not 99 per cent, it's less than that.

"But basically people are doing it on their gut feelings."

Loading...

AI superintelligence smarter than humans

Last week, two researchers warned that the rapidly progressing technology could lead to the extinction of the human race in the not-too-distant future.

Professor Hinton said most experts believed superintelligent AI would arrive within a decade, and that nobody knew whether it could be kept under control.

"Until we've solved that problem, it would be foolish to develop them."

Who can put the brakes on AI? AI might not kill us but it joins climate change and the nuclear threat in providing reasons to worry.

Some critics have argued that tech chief executives have played up the risks of AI to boost brand value and maintain the prestige of being a cutting-edge company.

Professor Hinton argued the opposite was true, saying that catastrophic warnings were bad for business.

"It's very silly marketing for the companies to say we might wipe you all out," he said.

"If there's a pause in AI, that may decrease the value of [Anthropic]."

The emeritus professor pioneered the neural network methods behind modern AI and left Google in May 2023 so he could speak freely about AI risk.

Globally, he said governments are regulating the technology far too slowly.

"Politicians act very slowly. It's going to be difficult to keep up.

" We've only got a few years. "

Another cyberattack linked to OpenAI agents Agents being tested by OpenAI uploaded hundreds of malicious packages to RubyGems in May, researchers have revealed.

Nuclear weapons, engineered viruses and mass manipulation

Asked how superintelligent AI could cause irreparable harm, Professor Hinton said there were too many possible routes to list: engineered viruses, mass manipulation, bringing down banking, power and water systems, or nuclear weapons, if AI ever reached the systems controlling them.

But he said that cataloguing them missed the point.

"The point is, we have to figure out how it never wants to."

Professor Hinton said systems had already shown, in safety testing, the behaviours researchers had warned about.

"We've seen them threatening to blackmail people if they're turned off," he said.

"They also develop deception. They develop all the kind of weaselly things that nasty people develop."

To mitigate risks, Professor Hinton suggested that governments could require pre-release testing before any chatbot model is released and oblige DNA synthesis firms to screen what they are asked to make.

"They can say that any company that manufactures chemicals on the web — where you send it a sequence of amino acids and it sends you back the protein — any company that does that should be obliged to check whether it's making nasty viruses."

Despite advising a slowdown, Professor Hinton told the ABC that AI was currently "doing tremendous good" by helping radiologists read images and assisting in the design of new drugs.

"I don't think we should stop developing it altogether."

Irish reunification 'natural', Trump says US President Donald Trump has vowed to pay a dividend if the Republican Party keeps control of Congress after midterm elections.

Trump rejects calls for a slowdown

US President Donald Trump brushed off concerns about the pace of AI development, saying he did not want to cede America's edge to China.

"We're leading China in AI," he said.

"We're the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins."

Other AI bosses, including OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and billionaire xAI owner Elon Musk, have endorsed Mr Amodei's proposal.

But when asked about whether the industry should slow down, or be more regulated, Mr Trump said "very negative forces" were raising ideas that "won't happen".

In a CBS interview on the weekend, Mr Amodei said the competition between US and Chinese AI companies was the "toughest dilemma" in trying to establish a "speed limit" on AI development.

"We shouldn't kid ourselves, because the incentives to pull ahead and the military advantage that you get from that are so large that the ability to check that the other side isn't cheating has to be ironclad," he said.

"So I think that's going to be the work of years and, honestly, I don't know if it's possible."

ABC/Reuters

title: Hundreds of jobs to go at Whyalla steelworks
text:
Hundreds of workers in Whyalla will lose their jobs as a result of a decision to permanently shut down the blast furnace at the South Australian regional city's steelworks.

It is expected the decision will mean 500 workers will be out of a job, as well as more than 100 contractors working at the site.

Workers at the Whyalla steelworks were informed about the decision this morning.

The blast furnace has been offline since April and, despite the best efforts of workers, they have not been able to restart it.

The coal-fired oven was used to melt iron ore into liquid pig iron, which was then turned into steel.

It comes as administrators KordaMentha and the state and federal governments look to finalise the sale of the business, which went into administration 19 months ago.

South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas is expected to reveal further details about the decision this afternoon, including potential job offers from other employers, such as BHP.

The blast furnace at the Whyalla steelworks has been shut down for months. (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

At the time the administration was announced in February 2025, Mr Malinauskas said the purpose of appointing KordaMentha was to "stabilise the business and seek to stop" job losses from occurring.

"For workers employed by OneSteel Manufacturing, that is workers at the steelworks itself, they will now have their futures assured," the premier said at the time.

"They're in a situation now where they're not going to wake up tomorrow and the administrator is making people redundant."

Mr Malinauskas qualified those comments by adding that there would be "a process that the administrator goes through and the new owners potentially will make their own decisions".

But he further added that "people working at the steelworks today will be working there tomorrow and into the foreseeable future".

Optimism to reality check

Since the cautious optimism of early 2025, the forecasts around the future of Whyalla had started to shift, with both the premier and the administrators speaking openly about potential redundancies.

"If it comes to pass that there is a requirement for redundancies or whatever that looks like, you can rest assured that we'll comply with our enterprise agreements, we'll work with the unions, we'll work with the state to manage that as best we can," KordaMentha partner Sebastian Hams said in May.

Peter Malinauskas and Tom Koutsantonis in February 2025 discussing the Whyalla steelworks crisis. (ABC News: Trent Murphy)

Talk of sizeable job losses had been brewing in recent days ahead of the premier's arrival in the regional city on Monday morning.

Mr Hams addressed workers in the presence of the premier, Treasurer Tom Koutsantonis and local MP Eddie Hughes.

"We won't be able to accommodate everyone," Mr Hams said.

"Our first option is redeployment, our second option is voluntary redundancy and then the third option is essentially forced redundancy."

A letter distributed to workers and sighted by ABC News confirmed the bleak prognosis, stating that steelmaking would "cease" until "new steelworks assets are constructed using modern steelmaking technologies".

"We have reviewed our operating model and level resourcing required across the entire OneSteel business," the letter stated.

"As a result of the closure and restructuring, some parts of the business will no longer exist, while others will have reduced employee numbers.

"There will be significantly fewer jobs available across the business. At this stage, we are anticipating potential impacts to approximately 500 employees and 100 labour hire workers."

"It is no longer appropriate to place our people at risk in pursuit of a recovery that is no longer feasible," it stated.

"We have therefore decided to cease attempts to restart the blast furnace."

Documents offering advice to workers who are set to lose their jobs are being circulated among the workforce, including training and financial advice and mental health support.

SA Treasurer Tom Koutsantonis was present at the meeting with workers. (Supplied)

According to the letter circulated to workers, a forum will be held in Whyalla this afternoon to allow contractors to ask questions about the situation.

In July, three steelworks employees were treated for injuries suffered during attempts to restart the site's troubled furnace — a situation alluded to in the letter to staff.

Sale still 'on track'

Two bidders, Jindal Steel and M Resources, remain in the running to buy the steelworks, but BlueScope Steel retains its right of last offer.

On Sunday, Mr Malinauskas said a sale was still likely in the next three and a half months.

"We intend to finalise the sale and the transaction by the end of this year. We're on track to do that," he said.

"What that will set up is a massive injection of capital into Whyalla to set it up for a new long-term future."

The blast furnace at the Whyalla steelworks emitting smoke during a shutdown. Photo taken September 14, 2026. (ABC News: Simon Goodes)

The SA government wrested control of the steelworks from Sanjeev Gupta's GFG Alliance in early 2025, in an extraordinary series of measures including urgent changes to the Whyalla Steel Works Act, which were rushed through both houses of state parliament.

GFG was in crisis after failing to pay tens of millions of dollars in royalty payments to the government, and millions in unpaid bills to creditors.

The current situation is the latest in a long line of moments of turmoil in the history of the steelmaking city.

In 2016 another previous owner, Arrium, went into voluntary administration after reporting a half-year loss of $236 million, including a $43 million loss for the Whyalla steelworks due to falling steel prices in Asia.

title: Promoter wins court battle over cancelled Robbie Williams gig
text:
Australian Grand Prix organisers have failed to overturn a $2.84 million compensation order to a music promoter over a COVID-era Robbie Williams concert cancellation.

A panel of three Court of Appeal justices backed the 2024 Victorian Supreme Court ruling today, unanimously refusing race organisers' bid to appeal.

The Formula One event at Melbourne's Albert Park in 2020 was axed hours before gates opened on March 13 due to the looming threat of COVID-19.

Williams, whose discography includes Let Me Entertain You and Angels, was to perform at Lakeside Stadium the following day as part of the event, but his concert was also cancelled.

Live music promoter World Touring Melbourne sued Grand Prix organisers in 2024 for breach of contract, claiming the concert was axed because the corporation provided misleading information about government health advice.

The 2020 Australian Grand Prix was cancelled while fans were already queued at the entrance gates. (ABC News: Simon Tucci)

Justice Clyde Croft ruled in 2024 that event organisers had deceived promoters by claiming Victoria's then chief health officer (CHO) Brett Sutton had directed the concert not to go ahead as planned, when no such advice had been given.

Organisers had emailed World Touring Melbourne at 4:25pm on March 13, stating Dr Sutton had advised the Grand Prix needed to be cancelled or run patron-free.

But the former CHO had actually texted Grand Prix officials earlier that day to say while he supported the decision to cancel the Williams concert, it was ultimately up to the organisers.

The judge ordered the Australian Grand Prix Corporation to pay $2.84 million in damages to World Touring Melbourne for loss of earnings.

Other events, including National Rugby League fixtures and a concert at Melbourne's Sidney Myer Music Bowl, continued that weekend.

AAP

title: NRL hands down decision on Cleary after finals sin-binning
text:
Nathan Cleary has avoided a ban for dangerous contact, with the Panthers star now just sweating on a foot injury ahead of Penrith's NRL preliminary final.

On Monday, Cleary was handed a grade-one dangerous contact charge for collecting Hugo Savala's leg after the Sydney Rooster kicked in Penrith's 19-12 qualifying final win.

But that charge only carries with it a $1,000 fine with an early guilty plea, meaning Cleary can breathe a sigh of relief with no ban in place.

Had Cleary been handed a grade-two charge, the Penrith halfback would have been facing a one-game ban and the reality of being rubbed out of the preliminary final.

Manly prop Josh Aloiai and South Sydney forward Jacob Host received grade-two charges in 2024 for making contact with kickers.

Canberra's Zac Hosking was fined for a similar incident in last year's finals, while Melbourne's Harry Grant had a charge overturned at the judiciary in 2024.

Loading Instagram content

With the threat of a ban now out of the way, Cleary can focus on his foot and the two weeks he has to be fit to take on the winner of the Warriors and Newcastle.

Cleary was easily Penrith's best in the win over the Roosters, but his sin-bin at the end of the first half for the contact on Savala was only the start of his worries.

The 28-year-old limped through the final 10 minutes of the game with a sore right foot, and opted to give Dylan Edwards the Panthers' last conversion attempt.

Cleary also appeared to say to a Penrith physio after kicking the match-winning 72nd-minute field goal, "my foot is f***ed".

The star half did attempt to play down the injury to his right foot after the game, but his father and coach Ivan admitted there was "something wrong with it".

"I just copped a little bump on the foot," Nathan Cleary said on Fox League.

"It was a pretty important kick, so I just wanted Dyl [Edwards] to take it. I wasn't sure how it would hold up goal kicking.

"It was just precautionary."

title: Antonelli edges closer to historic title as teammate concedes the fight
text:
Kimi Antonelli is on the brink of becoming the youngest F1 champion in history, while his nearest rival says he is out of the fight.

Antonelli's win in Madrid on Sunday night (AEST) was his eighth grand prix win of the season, extending his lead in the drivers' championship over teammate George Russell to 81 points.

Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton is a further 20 points adrift with eight or nine race weekends remaining, depending on whether F1 can race in the Middle East to end the season.

Piastri hit twice on first lap, Antonelli wins thanks to safety car luck Oscar Piastri and George Russell made contact with each other twice before the first corner, as Kimi Antonelli took full advantage of a fortunate safety car to win the Formula 1 Spanish Grand Prix.

Mercedes have lived up to pre-season expectation that they would be the best team in 2026 but Russell, in his eighth season, was expected to win a maiden drivers' championship.

But Antonelli, in just his second season, has been brilliant all season and has a massive lead in the championship.

After Sunday's Spanish Grand Prix, where Russell placed fifth and conceded a further 15 points to Antonelli, the British driver conceded his hopes of winning the title this year are all but gone.

"We [Mercedes] are in a great position to win the constructors' [championship]. Realistically, I'm not in the fight for the drivers'," Russell said in Madrid.

" That just allows me to focus on race-by-race, and try to focus on just getting some good results. "

Sebastian Vettel became the youngest F1 world champion in 2010 when he claimed his maiden title at 23 years, 133 days.

Antonelli took the mantle as youngest driver to lead the championship earlier this year — but when asked if he could relax with an 81-point lead, the young Italian said he would not be taking his foot off the gas.

"That's exactly what I don't want to do," he said.

"I want to keep pushing race by race, keep delivering and keep enjoying all the way."

F1 heads to Azerbaijan for a grand prix around the streets of Baku on Saturday, September 26.

title: 'It's for you, Mum': Cooney-Cross makes emotional Arsenal home return
text:
Matildas star Kyra Cooney-Cross has shared an emotional message from her late mother with fans as she made her return to the women's top flight in London.

The Australian star midfielder played her first Women's Super League game for Arsenal since late last year.

With the blessing of the club, she had taken personal leave early this year to be with her mother Jess.

Arsenal shows support for Cooney-Cross Arsenal players and supporters pay emotional tributes to Matildas star Kyra Cooney-Cross following her return to Australia to be with her mother, who has been diagnosed with cancer.

Cooney-Cross announced on January 8 via Instagram that her mother was diagnosed with terminal stage 4 bile duct cancer. She died on July 10.

Arsenal manager Renee Slegers confirmed on March 28 Cooney-Cross was granted indefinite compassionate leave and would remain in Australia after the Asian Cup to be with her mother.

Before the game against Crystal Palace, fans and teammates gave Cooney-Cross a big welcome.

In the end, Arsenal drew 0, leaving the club fifth on the Women's Super League table.

But it wasn't really about the result.

In the Arsenal match day program, Cooney-Cross wrote a personal note to the fans, thanking them for the "outpouring of love and support we received", saying it would never leave her or her family.

"Coming back to the UK was made easier because I have a family here," she wrote.

Cooney-Cross said her mum was very good at sending her messages before games, and so she shared a message from Jess "for all of us".

Loading Instagram content

"Kyra, try to remember what it felt like when you were little … when you just loved having the ball at your feet, playing with your mates, testing yourself against the boys or adults for the fun of it,' the message reads.

"Back then, it wasn't about proving anything … it was about the feeling, the freedom, the creativity, the joy of pushing yourself.

"Play because you love the ball at your feet, the rhythm of the game. Train because it feels good to move and challenge your body and feel strong.

"This is how you start doing it for you again — Mum."

Cooney-Cross finished her message with a simple line:

"It's for you, Mum. Love," and then her signature.

title: Ariarne Titmus among elite athletes dragging Sydney Sweeney betting ad
text:
Dozens of athletes have taken aim at a highly sexualised advertisement for a betting company featuring actress Sydney Sweeney, accusing it of belittling women in sport.

The ad shows Sweeney in little to no clothing as she plays mock tennis, golf, baseball and ice hockey, holds basketballs, footballs and a soccer ball, and boasts about punters being able to bet on "just sports".

"So they wanted to show just sports," she says while perched topless on top of a basketball hoop.

After saying "sports" nine times, she appears topless on a pool table, before saying: "You can't trade this, I just look good here."

Sydney Sweeney appears topless for most of the advertisement. (YouTube: Novig)

The advertisement has been widely criticised, particularly by female athletes, for setting back women in sport.

American gymnast Gracie Kramer was one of the first to respond with an Instagram reel reading: "idk what Sydney Sweeney was doing, but this is what a woman in sport looks like."

Loading Instagram content

"Because it really is that deep," she wrote in the caption, kicking off a trend among some of the best athletes around the world.

A slew of Australian Olympians are part of the chorus, with even the AIS posting: "THIS is sport", featuring several women athletes with the same backing track as the ad.

Swimming great Ariarne Titmus commented on the ad on Instagram, where it has been viewed over 33 million times, describing it as "an absolute joke".

Loading Instagram content

"I can't describe how infuriated I feel when I watch this," the four-time Olympic gold medallist wrote on her stories.

"Not only is it a kick in the face to every woman who has dedicated her life to perfecting her craft, but every woman who enjoys sports for what it really is — teamwork, friendship, dedication, excellence, unity … the list goes on.

"But how do we live in a world where monetising a woman's body and sexualising women's sport is still a thing? To take the mickey like this, I thought we were genuinely moving past this bullsh*t.

"What is this teaching young men and women of today? Sydney Sweeney, do better."

Loading Instagram content

Titmus's replacement as swimming's middle-distance queen, Lani Pallister, also posted that she had "truly no words", while Hockeyroos goalkeeper Joc Bartram said she was disappointed to see women's sport being sexualised.

"In a world where it just feels like women's sport is being recognised for the talent and skill that it involves rather than the sexualisation of women, this new add (sic) by @sydney_sweeney feels so out of touch," said Bartram, who was named goalkeeper of the tournament at the recent World Cup where the Hockeyroos finished fourth.

"There are so many different ways to get people's attention rather than sexualising women's sport once again. For another woman to bring female athletes down to such a level when we have fought so long to be recognised by our male counterparts and are still fighting to prove we belong every day, just leaves me speechless.

"There are so many incredible female athletes doing wonderful things for their sport and women's sport as a whole, please throw your support behind them rather than this tasteless campaign!"

Loading Instagram content

Australian Olympians like Bree Masters, Lauren Ryan and Liz Clay, and water polo silver medallist Tilly Kearns, were among those posting to highlight what women in sport actually look like.

"I absolutely fking hate Sydney Sweeney's new sports ad," Kearns said.

"Like what are we doing … so much worse than I imagined too."

Australian Olympic boxer and WBC bantamweight champion Skye Nicolson joined the trend while acknowledging the backlash was giving the company "exactly what they wanted".

Loading Instagram content

"But honestly these companies need to do better. Stop sexualising women in sport," she wrote.

In an apparent response to the criticism, Sweeney posted on her Instagram stories several images from ESPN's famous Body issue, showing numerous nude elite athletes, including tennis legend Serena Williams, UFC icon Ronda Rousey, NFL great Rob Gronkowski and NBA champion Karl-Anthony Towns.

This is not the first time Sweeney has faced criticism for an advertising campaign, including a 2025 American Eagle ad that boasted about her "great jeans" and was praised by US President Donald Trump.

The advertisements received backlash for alluding to eugenics and the belief in genetic superiority of blonde-haired, blue-eyed white people.

When asked about the backlash and criticism that "specifically in this political climate white people shouldn't joke about genetic superiority", Sweeney was non-committal.

"I think that when I have an issue that I want to speak about, people will hear," she told GQ.

Just as this controversy has boosted an otherwise little-known company into the international spotlight, the American Eagle controversy boosted the company's stock, although the apparel retailer has slumped recently.

title: Mary Gaudron, Australia's first female High Court judge, dies aged 83
text:
Pioneering Australian judge Mary Gaudron has been honoured for her contributions to Australia's legal landscape following her death at age 83.

Ms Gaudron became the first woman appointed to the High Court of Australia in 1987 at age 44 and served until 2003.

Her death was confirmed in multiple tributes posted online yesterday.

Loading Instagram content

While serving on the High Court, she contributed to decisions that shaped Australian law, including the landmark native title case, Mabo vs Queensland.

In the decision, Ms Gaudron and fellow High Court judge William Deane wrote of Aboriginal dispossession as "the darkest aspect of the history of this country".

Born on January 5, 1943, in the north-west New South Wales town of Moree, Ms Gaudron blazed a trail in a male-dominated profession.

After studying law at Sydney University on a scholarship and initially practising primarily in defamation and industrial law, she became the first woman appointed to the NSW Bar Council in 1972.

After stepping down from the High Court in 2003, Ms Gaudron took a job with the International Labour Organization in Geneva and became president of its administrative tribunal.

In 2000, she laid bare what she believed were the true views of some powerful men on women's equality.

"There are, I think, people who do not accept that men and women are equal, who do not think of equality as a good thing and, indeed, who actually fear the equal participation of women in the workplace," she said.

Governor-General Sam Mostyn said Ms Gaudron's legacy endured in the many people who followed the path she helped forge.

Mary Gaudron (left) with Julia Gillard, Quentin Bryce and Nicola Roxon in 2011, after the swearing-in ceremony of the new Gillard ministry. (AAP: Tracey Nearmy)

"As the first woman appointed to the High Court of Australia, and the only woman justice in the court's first century, she broke new ground and inspired generations of Australians to pursue careers in the law and public service," Ms Mostyn said in a social media post yesterday.

"Justice Gaudron brought her fierce intellect, integrity, compassion and a deep commitment to justice to every role she held.

"Her legacy endures in the Australian legal system and in the many people who continue to follow the path she helped forge."

Minister for Social Services Tanya Plibersek also paid tribute to Ms Gaudron, saying she "changed Australia's legal landscape".

"She fought for equal pay, broke down barriers for women in law … her intellect and courage made our country fairer," she said.

The Law Society of South Australia said Ms Gaudron's intellect, courage and commitment to justice helped shape the Australian legal landscape.

"Justice Gaudron made an enduring contribution to public life through her advocacy for equality, her service to the legal profession and her role as a trailblazer for women in law," Law Society president David Colovic said.

The High Court of Australia released a statement paying tribute to Ms Gaudron and her "distinguished career".

"Ms Gaudron advanced the role of women in the legal profession and in the judiciary by her advocacy as well as her example," the statement said.

"As a Justice of the High Court for 16 years, her impact on its institutional character and contribution to its work were profound."

AAP/ABC

title: One Nation unveils 'breathing space' plan for net-negative migration
text:
One Nation has unveiled its plan to slash immigration by 750,000 places over three years, with major cuts targeting international students and the families of skilled migrants.

Student visas would be capped at about a third of the current intake dipping to just over 100,000 places a year, with a new visa category created for "high-value" students, similar to US President Donald Trump's so-called "genius visas".

Visas for families of both international students and skilled migrants would be cut to zero and people who overstayed their visa would be banned from Australia for life.

The policy goes further than the party initially indicated, with migration levels going backwards for the first three years in what the party is calling "net-negative migration" to give Australians "breathing space".

After that, the party would pursue a "ceiling" of 130,000 in the net overseas migration program to be reviewed year on year.

Pauline Hanson says the proposal will give Australians "breathing room". (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said Australians had "had enough of mass migration" and accused the major parties of sacrificing living standards to "serve vested interests".

She said the plan would bring migration to 2017 levels of between 2.1 and 2.2 million people.

Labor frontbencher Murray Watt said the policy would "destroy regional economies" and "probably drive the Australian economy into recession".

"Apart from One Nation, we all recognise that we do have some serious labour shortages in some industries, and that is why coming out with these knee-jerk remarks can be a real economic problem," he said.

But Senator Hanson said a large economy meant "nothing" if Australians could not afford a home.

"A larger economic pie doesn't mean anything if individual Australians' slice of it is getting smaller," she said.

Labor frontbencher Murray Watt says the plan would likely cause a recession. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said it was still unclear what the net overseas migration (NOM) would be year on year under the One Nation program, but he was "deeply concerned" about the potential impact on business.

"They need to explain what their policies mean for hardworking small businesses in this country," he said.

"It's half-baked."

University places targeted

The proposal would slash international student places from 590,000 to 350,000.

Universities that provide student housing for international students, rather than relying on them to find their own arrangements in the private rental market, would be given priority.

The cuts would also target international graduates who wished to remain in Australia to work after they finished their studies, reducing the number from 270,000 to just 40,000.

Premier warns against 'race to bottom' on immigration The federal government is in discussions with the opposition over immigration as SA Premier Peter Malinauskas warns major parties against a "political race to the bottom".

There is also a new category for "high-value" students which would prioritise those with PhDs and science, engineering and frontier technology.

"Our new high-value postgraduate study visa will also help attract the world's brightest minds in science, engineering and medical research, giving Australia the talent we need to compete and returning universities to their proper role as research institutions rather than visa factories," Senator Hanson said.

Families of students on high-value visas would be allowed to apply for visas to come to Australia, but those on standard student visas would not.

One Nation's policy position paper said Australia would "continue to welcome international students" but said the sector should compete on the "quality of its education" with migration decisions "made separately in Australia's interests".

The proposed changes would also make it harder for international students to secure visas for some study areas deemed "oversupplied" including accounting, IT and business.

One Nation Treasury spokesperson Barnaby Joyce told News24 there were some universities "basically harvesting people" for the purpose of bringing them into Australia, not to create a graduate who could go on to contribute.

One Nation won't go 'door to door'

Mr Joyce said the party was not proposing "running around door to door" to find visa overstayers, but said they would "pop up".

Watch National Forum on ABC TV and iview David Speers puts the big questions on migration, multiculturalism and national identity to the people shaping the debate on Monday at 8:30pm AEST on ABC TV and ABC iview.

He would not put a number on negative NOM over the next three years because he said deportation was a complex process.

Asked today whether the policy would push Australia into recession, he claimed it would merely return the Australian economy to 2017 settings.

"We're going back to 2017 levels, and I don't think 2017 was a disaster for Australia," he told News24.

While Mr Joyce cited the 2017 economic example to argue there would be no negative impact, he also said he was confident house prices would not fall back to 2017 levels.

"And after three years we go back to our NOM ceiling of 130,000 after we've done the hard work, and then we get a more standard, effective and diligent way to bring people in," he said.

No pathway for skilled migrant families

Visas for skilled migrants are proposed by One Nation to remain uncapped and driven by "employer demand", and in-need skills like trades would be prioritised.

But visa places for families of skilled migrants would go to zero.

Earlier this year business groups rubbished a leaked Labor proposal to process families of skilled migrants offshore, which they said would make Australia a less attractive option for critical workers.

The Australian Chamber of Commerce said it did not support "wholesale cuts" to Australia's migration program to meet an "arbitrary net overseas migration number".

"Major cuts that reduce skilled migration would damage our economy, hit the budget and weaken our capacity to provide services for, and lift, living standards for Australians," it said in a statement.

Mr Joyce indicated family visas may be available to some skilled migrants on a "needs basis".

"If people have a needs basis in certain areas, that becomes a consideration of the visa application process," he said.

Business worried about possible immigration cuts Business and mining leaders are warning it is critical for Australia to remain a destination of choice for skilled migrants.

One Nation said it would retain settings for seasonal workers including the working holiday maker program and the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme, which many regional communities relied on.

National Farmers Federation chief executive Michael Guerin warned farm workers were not responsible for Australia's housing crisis and said migration should not be treated as "political football".

"International students also contribute to agriculture's workforce, particularly through casual and seasonal roles in regional areas, helping farms meet peak labour needs when local workers are not available," he said.

Do not travel ban remains

One Nation has stuck by its promise to pause migration from countries the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade rates as "do not travel" because of "terrorism or other extreme security risks".

Call for better migration policy An expert argues the migration debate is fixated on the wrong number while regional Australia calls for a national settlement strategy.

The party has previously promised to refuse entry to migrants from nations "known to foster extremist ideologies" that are "incompatible with Australian values and way of life".

Senator Hanson said she wanted to stop taxpayer-funded legal aid for visa appeals.

One Nation also has a policy to introduce an eight-year waiting period for citizenship and welfare, and promised to withdraw Australia from the UN Refugee Convention.

title: Team USA wins fifth straight Women's Basketball World Cup

Jackie Young added 18 points, six rebounds and five assists as the US used a dominant third quarter to close the door on France's chances.

France held a 20-17 lead after ‌the first ‌quarter following a 3-pointer from Marine Johannes and a pair of Malonga free throws.

title: Children experience 'profound disadvantage' in WA resource-rich area
text:
Every month, billions of dollars in trade is exported through Port Hedland, the iron ore-coated export hub in WA's Pilbara region.

But on the doorstep of the world's largest bulk export port, about 1,630 kilometres north of Perth, children in South Hedland are experiencing what has been described as "profound disadvantage".

The Pilbara has long been touted as the engine room of Australia's economy. So how is it that one of the wealthiest regions in Australia is seeing children go without, less than 15 kilometres down the road?

Port Hedland handles billions of dollars of trade each month. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne)

Tania Murray, chief executive of South Hedland's Youth Involvement Council (YIC), said the contrast was confronting.

"For some of our young people, it's going home to housing that is below acceptable standards, very little food, overcrowding, there's no adequate air conditioning, even though we live in a desert," she said.

" And at times there's very little sense of safety, and that's when poverty stops being an economic statistic. "

Pilbara to parliament

Working with locally based YIC, the Valuing Children Initiative's (VCI) End Child Poverty campaign captured the voices of children in South Hedland.

The kids' voices were recorded through a phone and will be played to federal ministers and MPs in Canberra today.

Tania Murray says it is important to hear directly from the children. (Supplied: Valuing Children Initiative)

"When the researchers from VCI came up, our job wasn't to research what children in Hedland experience; our job was to create a safe opportunity for children to tell themselves," Ms Murray said.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics' Socio-Economic Indexes for Areas (SEIFA), a tool that ranks areas according to their relative socio-economic advantage and disadvantage based on census data, South Hedland's score was 989, lower than the broader Port Hedland area average of 1,011.

Children in South Hedland have been asked about the issues they are facing. (Supplied: Valuing Children Initiative)

End Child Poverty campaign lead and VCI executive director Sarah Quinton said it was important that children were asked about their experiences directly.

"We were invited to South Hedland by the Youth Involvement Council because they were so concerned about the number of children that they were seeing," she said.

" They're talking about 500 children that they see who come to their service and they were saying that they're very hungry all the time, they haven't eaten, they haven't slept, they haven't gone to school. "

Calls for national strategy

WA Commissioner for Children and Young People Jacqueline McGowan-Jones said she was not surprised by the findings.

"There's a two-speed economy. There's all the money going out every day in the port; children see that and they understand it," she said.

"We know from talking to children themselves, that this is a critical issue … I've spoken to elders, I've spoken to community groups, I've spoken to the Aboriginal community-controlled organisations, and we know there is more to be done."

Jacqueline McGowan-Jones says there needs to be a greater response. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

Ms Quinton said there needed to be a nationally legislated strategy to end child poverty that included a definition and metrics for children.

"We might have measures like CPI, we might have mortgage rates, those kinds of things, those are very adult-centred poverty measures," she said.

"Seeing the world from a child's point of view is so much different from an adult's point of view, we need to start measuring that.

" We need to be sitting down and really listening to children and bringing out those child-centred poverty indicators. "

'Come and see it'

Dr McGowan-Jones echoed calls for a nationally legislated poverty reduction strategy.

"We've got to stop blaming kids for the circumstances they're born into over which they have no control," she said.

"By not supporting them, by not providing the services and supports, we're basically saying, 'You don't matter.'"

In a statement, a spokesperson for the federal Department of Social Services said the government was working to break the cycle of disadvantage and improve the wellbeing of children.

"We know children and families in regional and remote areas like the Pilbara can face unique barriers," the spokesperson said.

"Children and families in the area have access to programs designed to improve wellbeing and connection."

The Youth Involvement Council, based in South Hedland, works with young people. (Supplied: Valuing Children Initiative)

Ms Murray called on decision-makers to see the issues firsthand.

"My message to the people in Canberra is to come and see it," she said.

"Most importantly, sit down with our young people and listen to them."

title: Working holiday visa pause leaves farms short as harvest season looms
text:
Farmers are worried there won't be enough workers to pack fruit and harvest crops after recent changes to visa processing.

The federal government has paused working holiday visa applications coming from 24 of 29 countries, amid a slowdown in processing skilled visa applications.

These two quiet changes, made to curb net overseas migration, have raised fears in the agricultural sector.

Operating heavy machinery is a key part of grain and crop harvest across Australia. (ABC Mid West and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Victorian contractor Matt Bourke had planned to hire 30 staff members ahead of the grain harvest in just a few weeks, with many coming from overseas on both visas.

"Not one working holiday visa has been approved yet," Mr Bourke said.

"There are probably 60 or 70 per cent who have worked with me in the past. I've never had this issue before."

Working holiday visas

The National Farmers Federation estimates that overseas workers make up about half of Australia's peak harvest casual workforce.

Agricultural workers predominantly use two types of visas to apply for seasonal harvest jobs: the work and holiday visa for backpackers, and the skilled visa for skilled workers like heavy machinery operators.

The Australian government's Department of Home Affairs website shows application cap indicators for the Working Holiday Maker (WHM) program. (Image: ABC News)

In a statement, a Department of Home Affairs spokesperson said the number of working holiday-makers (WHMs) in Australia was at a historically high level.

As a result, "applications may take longer than usual and may be finalised outside the published processing time frames."

As of June 30, 2025, there were 206,187 working holiday-makers in Australia.

But despite the high figures, farmers across the country say they're struggling to recruit pickers.

In the Northern Territory, Berry Creek mango packing manager Phillipa Johnson said she was still looking for workers just a few weeks out from harvest.

Because it's a short two-to three-month season, many of her workers come from overseas on a working holiday visa.

Farm workers from overseas are crucial during the harvest season. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"We're getting some applications from overseas, but their visas haven't been approved," Ms Johnson said.

" We're going to have to go back to the drawing board. "

Skilled workers needed

In July, the Department of Home Affairs issued a new ministerial direction prioritising skilled visa processing for defence and law enforcement workers, followed by construction, healthcare, teaching, and people already in Australia.

While many farmers use working holiday visa applicants on their farm for a seasonal workforce, other farmers need specific skills they can't find in Australia.

Mr Bourke said professionally trained skilled workers had been vital to his operation over the harvest period.

"The guys we're bringing into the country are currently running those machines at home, in their own country, on their own farms or on farms around them," he said.

" They are here for good reason because the availability of this labour is not here in Australia. "

Earlier this year, Tasmanian dairy farmer Michele Lawrence gave evidence to the parliamentary inquiry into the value of skilled migration in Australia.

Meander Valley dairy farmer, Michele Lawrence. (Supplied: Michele Lawrence)

The chair of People and Communities Policy Advisory at Australian Dairy Farmers spoke about the essential role overseas workers on both visas play in sustaining dairy production and food security.

"We need these people; the working holiday-makers will stay on our farm for as long as they can on their visas," she said.

Ms Lawrence employs several working holiday makers on her Meander Valley property, and said she's still waiting for an ag science engineer to arrive from Argentina.

"Within that we've got a skill set of science degrees, nursing degrees and electrical trades," she said.

"They're really strategic people on our farm."

No clarity on delays

A Department of Home Affairs spokesperson said it was taking a range of measures to put pressure on overseas migration, better manage demand for the WHM program, and support a fairer allocation of visas.

"These actions will be rolled out progressively to ensure the long-term sustainability of the WHM program while continuing to support the tourism economy and workforce needs, particularly in regional Australia," they said.

"Visa applicants are advised not to arrange travel to Australia until they have been notified in writing of the grant of their visa."

title: Alexander Zverev wins US Open without realising it
text:
Alexander Zverev has won his second grand slam title of 2026, beating American Ben Shelton in four sets to claim the US Open in New York.

Zverev, who won his first major crown at this year's French Open, wrapped up the 6-3, 7-6(7/2), 5-7, 6-2 victory over Shelton in three hours and 33 minutes but he did not even realise he had won in the moment.

After banging down another unreturnable serve at 40-15 in the eighth game of the fourth and final set, the German simply turned to prepare to return, before he realised what had happened when he looked up at the big screen.

"I thought it was 5-1, which helped me. I probably would've served like three double faults instead of one," he told ESPN.

"But it was a long match, a long two weeks. In the end I'm happy."

When it eventually clicked for the 29-year-old, he said, "I've won?" with a smile, and rushed to the net to commiserate with first-time finalist Shelton before the celebrations began.

"We went 30 years without winning a grand slam title and now we've won two in the span of three months," Zverev said.

Zverev said he would "bet all [his] money" that 23-year-old Shelton would lift the trophy one day, but it was not to be this day.

Both teams have strong family connections in their coaches' box, with Shelton coached by father Bryan, and his mother and sister also among his supporters in the stands.

Ben Shelton had the crowd on his side at his first grand slam final. (Getty Images: Simon Bruty/USTA)

"It's exactly what my family is and that's why I'm so happy to see you guys in these kinds of finals," Zverev said.

As he was looking around Shelton's supporters, Zverev spied US football star Trinity Rodman, Shelton's girlfriend who rushed from her Washington Spirit's 3-0 loss to Boston in DC to see the end of the match.

Zverev described her as Shelton's "lucky charm", to which she replied: "Clearly not."

The world number two also took time to thank former Australian Open director Craig Tiley after his first US Open as United States Tennis Association boss.

"He decided to move to New York, which we as players were not very happy about because he made the Australian Open the best tournament in the world," he said.

"But from now on I think the US Open will probably be the best tournament in the world since you're here. Thank you for moving here, thank you for being here, [but] move back to Australia for like three months and come back at the end of January. That would be great."

Playing his sixth major final and second in New York, Zverev looked composed as he took the opening set 6-3 in just 40 minutes on the back of a 94 per cent win rate on first serves.

Alexander Zverev lost from two sets up in the 2020 US Open final. (Getty Images: Simon Bruty/USTA)

In a battle between two of the best servers on tour, neither could get a break as the second set went to a tiebreak, where the more experienced campaigner dominated, jumping out to a 5-0 lead before taking it 7-2.

There would have been no complacency, though, as Zverev lost the 2020 US final to Dominic Thiem after winning the first two sets.

Shelton showed his fighting spirit to claim the third with his only service break and extend the match, but he was quickly broken to start the fourth set and Zverev raced to a 5-2 lead with a second break, setting up his victorious moment that clearly came earlier than he expected.

Sarytogan Graphite has reached a major milestone in its downstream processing ambitions, producing high-quality, battery-grade coated spherical purified graphite (CSPG) that smashed key industry specifications for use in lithium-ion batteries. Testwork on a 24-tonne bulk sample from its massive deposit in Central Kazakhstan has delivered a hefty 97.7 per cent yield, towering over the typical industry range of 50 to 60 per cent. A high yield is crucial to production economics, putting more of every tonne of mined graphite into high-value battery anode material and leaving less behind as lower-value product. Sarytogan has produced high-quality coated spherical purified graphite (pictured) from its giant deposit in Kazakhstan, exceeding key lithium-ion battery specifications. Perhaps even more significantly, the end product reached a whopping purity greater than 99.99 per cent – the coveted “four nines” mark – comfortably eclipsing the typical 99.95 per cent lithium-ion battery requirement. Sarytogan also knocked it out of the park on tap density, chalking up between 0.99 and 1.26 grams per cubic centimetre (g/cm³), a hefty improvement on its previous testwork and pushing well beyond the typical industry benchmark of about 1g/cm³. Tap density essentially measures how tightly graphite particles can pack together, with higher numbers potentially translating into more energy being squeezed into a battery. The company’s processor noted that tap densities above 1.2g/cm³ are considered “very rare” in the battery industry and are prized for their potential to enable higher energy densities in batteries.

Advertisement

‘Small sphere sizes with ultra-high tap densities are highly prized in the lithium-ion battery.’ Sarytogan Graphite managing director Sean Gregory The testwork, conducted by specialist American Energy Technologies Company in the US, produced approximately 30 kilograms of various downstream products, including ultra-high-purity fines, uncoated spherical purified graphite, and the all-important CSPG. The results are a significant step in the company’s strategy to become a vertically-integrated supplier of graphite to the burgeoning electric vehicle and energy storage markets. Sarytogan is now preparing a 5kg CSPG sample to ship to a leading European battery prototyping organisation. The material will be used to manufacture and test 5-amp-hour, large-format pouch-cell batteries, a significant scale-up from previous successful coin-cell tests and a key step in qualifying the product for potential European offtake partners. Sarytogan managing director Sean Gregory said: “These scaled-up purification, spheroidization, and coating results are an important step forward in the development of Sarytogan’s downstream graphite products. Small sphere sizes with ultra-high tap densities are highly prized in the lithium-ion battery for their associated fast-charging and high-energy-densities respectively.”

Advertisement

The company’s processing pathway, which it calls an “inverted flowsheet”, involves purifying the graphite before spheroidization. This is a clever piece of process design, as it means any graphite particles that don’t meet the size or shape specifications during spheroidization can still be sold as a premium ultra-high purity product, rather than a lower-value concentrate. All this is happening against the backdrop of Sarytogan’s colossal mineral resource, which stands at 225 million tonnes grading a remarkably high 29.2 per cent total graphitic carbon. The deposit’s scale and grade have not gone unnoticed on the world stage, with the project having been designated a Strategic Project under the European Union’s Critical Raw Materials Act, highlighting its potential as a vital future supplier to Europe. With an upstream definitive feasibility study for the mine and initial processing plant now in its final stages and due for release next quarter, the company appears to be methodically piecing together a mine-to-market plan. Meanwhile, 25 kilometres away, Sarytogan’s Baynazar copper project recently delivered the goods with a 229 metre copper hit grading 0.14 per cent copper from surface to end of hole. The impressive hit came from the Ilskan prospect and confirms the presence of a copper porphyry-style mineralised system. The company is now eagerly awaiting results from two other diamond drill holes at Ilskan. The latest downstream results provide strong proof of concept that Sarytogan’s world-class deposit can be transformed into a world-class battery product. A landmark federation home on one of Brisbane’s best streets has clinched the nation’s top auction result of the weekend after selling for $17 million. Built in early circa 1900s, the six-bedroom estate sits on a 2,024-square-metre parcel at 1 Sutherland Avenue, Ascot, and has remained in the same family for 25 years. Four buyers registered for the Saturday auction, including two locals and two virtual bidders who phoned in from Sydney and the US. In front of a crowd at the Calile Hotel, bidding opened at $12 million with three bidders trading mostly $1 million rises. At $16.8 million, two remained and the auction paused – before selling under the hammer moments later. Ray White Collective’s Matt Lancashire marketed the home, and while unable to disclose buyer details, he said the result showed Brisbane’s defiance in the face of grim national property headlines.

Advertisement

“The campaign was amazing. We had close to 100 groups through in three weeks but when you’ve got a landmark once-in-a-generation home like this that’s why,” he said. “Houses on Sutherland Avenue just don’t come up often and it’s generally regarded as one of Brisbane’s best streets. “But this result also tells me that Brisbane’s high-end market is in good nick. “We had 10 (interested) buyers with the capacity to spend that money. The issue is there’s no stock for them to buy.” The Ascot property sits a stone’s throw from Brisbane’s second most expensive home – 32 Sutherland Avenue – which smashed the city’s price ceiling when it fetched $23 million in late 2024. In 2025, an unrenovated riverfront home at 17 Julius Street, New Farm, reset the record at $25 million.

For vendor Donna Scott-Young, the sale marks the end of a deeply personal chapter. Together with her family, Scott-Young bought the home for just $1.66 million in 2001 and project managed a three-year renovation in 2007. “The home is just faultless … and it has a real soul,” said Lancashire said. “You simply couldn’t replace it even if you tried.” The Ascot property was one of 159 scheduled auctions across South East Queensland over the past week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary clearance rate of 32 per cent from 115 reported results, with 16 homes withdrawn. In Camp Hill, a four-bedroom, two-bathroom house on a 316-square-metre parcel at 16 Grant Street sold for $2.27 million in “textbook” auction, going to a young local. A buyer’s agent opened bidding at $1.9 million, sparking a flurry of $20,000 and $10,000 rises among the four registered bidders. Despite matching every bid with a quick $1000 rise, the buyers’ agent was forced to admit defeat at $2.231 million, leaving the young man to nab the keys. “Usually buyers agents’ open quite strong to try and knock people out but this one didn’t. Their clients may have thought a deal was to be had - but good properties are still selling for fair market price,” said Shane Hicks of Place Camp Hill. “And this was a textbook circa 2025 auction … it went like clockwork and the price was right in the middle of the range we were hoping to get.”

Run across 17 days, Hicks said the campaign showed an emerging market trend. “We had 15 groups through the first Saturday and at the second we had just four. So that tells us the depth of buyers isn’t as deep it was, but that the serious buyers are there,” said Hicks. “And they’re getting all the listing notifications and acting quickly.” While Hicks deemed the auction a win for both the buyer and seller, he said market sentiment remained a headwind. “Buyer confidence is probably the biggest difference between the 2025 and the 2026 market,” he said.

“Worst case scenario we’re seeing homes sell for 5 per cent less (than the peak) … but the biggest battle right now is trying to give buyers and sellers confidence in the market.” Nearby at 43 Princess Street in Bulimba, a Cleveland couple outmuscled four other bidders to nab a “rare” four-bedroom home built by Shaun Lockyer and Black Developments – paying $4,370,000. Bought off the plan in 2021 for $3.18 million, the home sits a stone’s throw from Oxford Street on a 759-square-metre parcel and features an outdoor barbecue kitchen, a pool and a media room. Bidding opened at $3.8 million, and a sluggish, hour-long contest followed before the hammer fell.

“Buyers are certainly being a bit more measured with their bidding … and I think every seller is wanting a bit more for their homes but the vendors were satisfied with the result,” selling agent Scott Darwon of Ray White Bulimba said. “We’re seeing that when the properties are priced right to the market they are receiving OK inquiry and attendance at auction … but everyone is across the news and buyers are being choosy. Despite market uncertainty, Darwon said about 80 groups inspected the home thanks to its location and pedigree. “It was the sheer quality of the home. In music there was Lennon and McCartney and in Brisbane (for architectural builds) it’s Lockyer and Black,” he said. LJ Hooker chief of research Matthew Tiller said Brisbane was continuing to outperform Sydney and Melbourne, with a lack of new listings adding a bit more buoyancy.

NationalVictoriaDisability Stroke victim Peter would be lost without the funding that paid for his scooter. Now it’s been slashed Benjamin Preiss September 14, 2026 — 11:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Peter Barry was about to start an exciting new chapter in his life. He was preparing to sell his house in Colac, in Victoria’s south-west, and take a job driving heavy machinery and trucks in the West Australian mining industry. His son’s family had already moved there and lined up work for Barry. But things didn’t go to plan. A stroke changed Peter Barry’s life, but his NDIS support has reduced despite his needs. Justin McManus Just before he was due to leave in May 2019, Barry found himself lying on the floor after falling while taking a coffee cup to the kitchen sink. He dragged himself into his bedroom and stood up using the bed for support, but when he walked into the laundry, he fell again, this time cutting his head and arm on the way down.

Advertisement

“I’m laying on my back talking to myself. ‘Get up, get up, you silly bastard’,” he said. “And I couldn’t.” Barry didn’t realise that he was having a stroke. A friend found him, and he was rushed to hospital, where he learnt that at 58, he was paralysed down on his left side. Barry at home with (from left) support worker Ella Williams and support co-ordinators Prue Muvengi and Ellie McInnes. Justin McManus Though he has since regained limited movement and can now hold jars with his left hand to open them, the stroke had a profound impact on Barry’s life. He can no longer work, lost his truck licence and now drives a modified car. Despite the life-changing effect of the stroke, Barry said support from the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) enabled him to regain some independence – particularly through the provision of a motorised scooter he uses to make trips to the shops.

Advertisement

“I’d be lost without this thing,” he said. When it opened in 2013, Colac was among the first locations in Victoria to get its own NDIS office where participants and support workers could speak to staff in-person. But a recent unexplained closure for about a month has raised questions and hampered the scheme’s ability to support the community. An NDIS office in Colac closed for a month suddenly and without explanation. Shutterstock CoConnect, a Colac-based not-for-profit group which supports more than 250 people across the south-west navigate the NDIS, said the temporary closure came without warning and was an unwelcome surprise to many. “We just showed up and no one was there,” CoConnect support co-ordinator Prue Muvengi said.

Advertisement

A spokesperson for the NDIS said its Colac office was closed due to maintenance required on heating. However, other government tenants of the same building, including Centrelink, continued operating in the same space throughout the same period. Related Article Exclusive

Disability Disability provider hit by strikes as funding gap bites Victorian Liberal MP Richard Riordon said the unexplained office closure in his electorate of Polwarth was not good enough. “The unplanned closure caused great distress to many clients and client advocates who require in-person meetings and advisory,” Riordan said. He noted the closure came at the same time as transport services in the Colac area were cut for 70 residents of group homes. Though the NDIS office has since resumed operating with staff present, Muvengi said the closure had created stress and confusion for clients.

Advertisement

She said there were previous instances where the NDIS had advised her over the phone that it could not find or accept forms she had submitted online, and she had to attend the local office. The temporary closure also came on the back of Muvengi’s concerns about reductions to funding packages for Colac people living with a disability, which is complicating efforts to provide them with the support they need. Barry, pictured with support co-ordinator McInnes, says he’d be lost without his motorised scooter. Justin McManus Barry estimates his funding package has been slashed roughly in half since his stroke in 2019. While he said the first package was generous and he did not use all his funding allocation, his in-home support hours had since been reduced from two hours daily to six hours a week over three days. His funding package no longer allows for supports including a pool membership, where he could have aquatic rehabilitation.

title: Geological smoke leads PLC Resources to bigger WA gold target
text:

Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Geological smoke leads PLC Resources to bigger WA gold target Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Penny Taylor September 14, 2026 — 11:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

PLC Resources has kicked off follow-up reverse-circulation (RC) drilling at its Rochefort gold prospect, part of the company’s Abbotts North gold project in Western Australia’s Murchison region, chasing what it believes could be a larger gold system lurking beyond its maiden drill pattern. An eight-hole, 2400m campaign will target northwestern and down-dip extensions of the prospect, where earlier drilling revealed strengthening gold values and a suite of geological and geochemical clues, suggesting the first holes may have clipped the edge of a bigger mineralised system. PLC Resources has started follow-up RC drilling at its Rochefort gold prospect in Western Australia’s Murchison region. The earlier five-hole, 1020m reconnaissance campaign, reported in July and representing the first modern gold drilling at the grassroots Rochefort, returned anomalous gold up to 0.4 grams per tonne (g/t) in three of five holes. The gold was hosted within highly fractionated dolerite alongside alteration, sulphidation and pathfinder geochemistry that PLC says warranted a closer look. The hotspot had already left a trail before drilling, with a 400m by 350m gold-in-soil anomaly and quartz-hematite vein rock chips grading up to 11.7g/t gold.

Advertisement

‘We’ve built a strong technical case for a larger gold system beyond our maiden drilling that all point to the northwest and at depth.’ PLC Resources executive director Simon Phillips Subsequent analysis gave PLC more indicators to follow. The company says gold values increase northwest and with depth alongside increasingly evolved dolerite, while sodic alteration interpreted as albitisation, magnesium depletion and weak but persistent sulphides, predominantly pyrrhotite, strengthen in the same direction. Multi-element work has added another pointer, withsulphur levels rising alongside elevated gold whilearsenic and antimony become relatively depleted. PLC believes the association indicates increasing proximity to a mineralising fluid pathway rather than a distal dispersion halo. The host rocks add another dash of geological spice. PLC says fractionated dolerites can make prime hunting ground for orogenic gold, pointing to Kalgoorlie’s famed Golden Mile dolerite as a geological cousin where evolved rocks often channel gold-bearing fluids before helping squeeze out their precious cargo. PLC Resources executive director Simon Phillips said: “It’s great to have the rig turning again at Rochefort. We’ve built a strong technical case for a larger gold system beyond our maiden drilling that all point the same way, to the northwest and at depth. This program is designed to directly test that target.”

Advertisement

Management expects PLC to complete the campaign in 14 days and will provide updates as drilling progresses. First assays are anticipated in four to six weeks, with results to follow as they are received and validated. The program is covered by existing environmental and heritage approvals and will be funded from existing cash reserves. In parallel, the company will continue advancing a newly interpreted regional structural corridor across its roughly 400-square-kilometre Abbotts North project. Geophysics identified a previously unmapped fold extending for more than 14km along the eastern margin of the greenstone belt that had not been recognised on existing government geological maps. The fold’s hinge intersects a deep-seated crustal structure – geological plumbing PLC regards as a first-order gold targeting feature. The company says such features can provide long-lived pathways for mineralising fluids, while their intersections can create favourable sites for those fluids to focus and deposit gold. The historic Abbotts goldfield has a strong pedigree, with records showing production of 41,000 ounces at a head grade of roughly 31g/t, principally from shallow quartz reefs. Large parts of the district have since seen little systematic modern exploration. Rochefort also sits 21km north of New Murchison Gold’s Garden Gully project in the same Abbotts Greenstone Belt. Garden Gully contains a 4.42-million-tonne resource at 2.5g/t gold for 359,300 ounces and hosts its producing Crown Prince gold mine.

PLC’s maiden drilling may not have delivered headline grades, but management believes it handed the company something potentially more useful – a geological treasure map. The next batch of holes will find out whether those clues lead to the main event. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

title: Barnaby Joyce reveals more details on One Nation's plan to cut migration
text:
In brief One Nation has announced a plan to slash Australia's temporary migrant population by 750,000 over three years.

The policy has been criticised by government and Opposition figures as damaging for the economy.

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce said his party will cut Australia's migrant population "primarily by not issuing new" visas, after his party announced a plan to dramatically slash migration and bring it into "net-negative" for three years on Monday.

The policy would cut Australia's temporary migrant population by 750,000 over three years — a move One Nation says would ease pressure on housing and essential services and return the temporary migrant population to 2017 levels.

It includes cuts to student visas, graduate visas, temporary skilled visas and bridging visa holders, as well as the "departure and removal of illegal migrants".

In an interview with News24, Joyce said not allowing the family of temporary skilled workers to apply to join their partners or parents in Australia will cut down migration by more than 100,000 people.

"We bring up [the example of] nurses thinking, Oh well, that’s 50 per cent, or 30 per cent [of skilled migrants]. No, it’s 1 per cent or less, the nurses, and less than 1 per cent is aged care workers.

"We’re getting numbers down primarily by not issuing new visas."

In 2025 the Australian Nursing and Midwifery Foundation reported internationally qualified nurses (IQNs) make up approximately 20 per cent of the total nursing workforce and in aged care this increases to 35 per cent.

Joyce also said universities are being used as a "backdoor" to migration, adding Australia is "going from a country to a caravan park".

"We're still having students come in. We're looking at a cap of 100,000 a year, but we're just not having this sort of universities used as basically a backdoor to migration into Australia," he said.

READ MORE Why fixing Australia's immigration system is not just about cutting migrants

Following the "three-year reset", where more people would leave Australia than arrive, One Nation says its annual cap of 130,000 on net overseas migration (NOM) would remain in place and be reviewed each year.

Net overseas migration measures the difference between the number of people who arrive in Australia and those who depart, including returning Australians.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke delayed a National Press Club speech in August in which he was widely expected to announce migration cuts. It is understood the cabinet is still finalising plans.

The government previously set a target of 225,000 for 2027-28.

Party leader Pauline Hanson said her plan was about "restoring control and making sure migration serves Australia".

The proposal expands on One Nation's existing migration policy after the party was forced to clarify its position in recent weeks following confusion sparked by comments from One Nation MP David Farley.

'A real shock to the economy'

Members of both Labor and the Coalition criticised the plan in Monday morning media appearances.

Health Minister Mark Butler said the plan would devastate the health and aged care sectors and smash certain industries like construction.

"Pauline Hanson said a few weeks ago, she didn't care what the impact of her migration policy would be on business, but this is just another level entirely," Butler told reporters on Monday.

Meanwhile, deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume told News24 a negative NOM would be a "real shock to the economy and it would make all Australians poorer".

"My concern here is that these numbers have simply been plucked out of thin air, that there isn't any modelling behind them," she said.

Both major parties have sought to restrict their own migration policies, though they've denied those moves are linked to One Nation's growing popularity.

When borders reopened following COVID-19 pandemic closures, Australia saw a surge in arrivals, with net overseas migration peaking at 556,000 in 2022-23.

NOM fell to 301,000 in 2025-26, according to data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

title: Swedish election in dead heat as anti-immigration far right loses ground
text:
In brief Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has headed a minority coalition backed by the far right Sweden Democrats for four years.

The election results will decide whether Kristersson's push toward a hard-right clampdown on migration continues.

Sweden's leftwing opposition bloc held a razor-thin lead in Sunday's general election with half of the votes counted, with the far right seen losing ground.

With more than 50 per cent of votes counted, four opposition parties led by Social Democratic leader Magdalena Andersson, had a narrow lead with 49.3 per cent against 49.1 per cent for Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's right-wing alliance, which includes the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats.

In a big surprise, the anti-immigration Sweden Democrats lost support for the first time since it entered parliament in 2010, with 17.7 per cent of the vote, down from 20.5 per cent in 2022.

"Of course it's a bit of a disappointment that we are not the second-biggest party anymore in these polls. But it's still not finished, it can still change," Julia Kronlid, a Sweden Democrat member of parliament, told Agence France-Presse (AFP) just after exit polls had showed the party retreating.

Experts predicted the race could go down to the wire.
