title: The hidden $140 billion economy helping some Australians get ahead
text:
Key Points Three in 10 homeowners say they received family help to buy, up from about one in 10 four years ago.

From free childcare to groceries and bills, family support is reshaping what financial independence looks like.

From free childcare to home deposits, groceries and holidays, billions of dollars are flowing between Australian generations long before an inheritance is handed down.

For Shane and Catherine, being grandparents to 10 children can sometimes resemble a full-time job.

A busy week can involve seeing one or more of their grandchildren almost every day, from picking them up from school, taking them to sport, helping with homework and cooking for them.

The couple, who have both worked as educators for 45 years, made a conscious decision to become active grandparents.

Catherine even reduced her working hours so she could help care for their grandchildren while their parents worked full-time.

"They couldn't have managed five days a week childcare. It's so expensive today," Catherine told SBS's Insight.

"So to look after the children, that's a saving in hundreds of dollars for them."

There may be no money changing hands, but the arrangement has significant financial value.

And Shane and Catherine are part of a much bigger, and often largely invisible, flow of support between Australian generations.

What is the 'Booster Economy'?

New research from SBS CulturalConnect estimates older Australians provide more than $140 billion worth of everyday financial support to younger family members each year.

The research involved in-depth interviews with 50 parents and grandparents providing support, followed by a survey of around 2,500 Australians.

More than 12 million Australians were found to support younger adult family members in some way.

Researchers have dubbed it the "Booster Economy", or the wealth and financial support flowing between generations while parents and grandparents are still alive.

And it extends far beyond the familiar "Bank of Mum and Dad" helping children into the housing market.

Among those providing support, 34 per cent had bought groceries for younger family members, 33 per cent had paid for restaurant meals and 30 per cent had bought clothes.

Almost one in five had paid for travel, while 14 per cent had bought a car and the same proportion had purchased appliances or electronics.

Forty-two per cent had provided cash, while 19 per cent had helped pay off debt.

The $140 billion estimate excludes cash transfers, debt repayments, homes and home deposits, capturing instead the scale of everyday purchases being made by older Australians for younger family members.

The Bank of Mum and Dad is getting bigger

Finder personal finance expert Sarah Megginson said its research suggests reliance on family wealth is already growing significantly in one of the biggest areas of household finances: housing.

Finder recently found 30 per cent of homeowners surveyed had received family assistance to purchase their property.

Contributions towards a deposit were the most common form of support, while 8 per cent said their family had paid for their home outright.

But Megginson said the change over time was particularly striking.

"About four years ago, those stats were looking like 10 per cent — like one in 10 were getting help from their parents," she told SBS News.

"Last year it came back around 20 per cent ... and now we're at three in 10.

"So we've just seen that trend continue to get even deeper year on year."

Megginson said older Australians were increasingly seeing the financial pressures facing their children and grandchildren and reconsidering when they passed on their wealth.

"Instead of the more traditional path of leaving an inheritance after they've gone, they've actually started, I guess, releasing it early," she said.

While housing deposits were a major example, Megginson said parents were also contributing towards expenses such as private school fees and other significant lifestyle costs.

From inheritance to everyday expenses

Megginson said the financial relationship between parents and their adult children had also changed considerably within a generation.

"I'm in my 40s, and I moved out and bought my first home in my early 20s, and that was the end of any kind of money relationship with my parents," she said.

"I was a grown-up then, paid for all of my own things."

But Megginson said younger colleagues in their 20s and 30s had described parents continuing to pay for things such as restaurant meals, or covering the cost of their children and their partners joining family holidays.

"I think that has been a huge generational shift," she said.

Housing affordability was one of the major forces behind the change, Megginson said, with the gap between incomes and property prices widening significantly over recent decades.

The report by Financial Services Council proposes changes that would see the amount of superannuation benefits left each year as a bequest halved by 2060, ensuring superannuation is primarily used up as income for retirement. Source: AAP / Moodboard

She said she increasingly heard from Australians who believed that without an inheritance or help from their parents, they would "simply never own a home".

Finder research has also found one in 10 Australians say they will need an inheritance to achieve a major financial goal, such as buying a property.

What if your parents can't afford to help?

But access to the Booster Economy is far from universal.

The SBS research highlights a stark difference between younger Australians whose families can provide significant support and those without the same financial safety net — including some who instead provide support to older relatives.

The consequences can extend beyond the immediate value of the help.

Regular free childcare, for example, can save a family hundreds of dollars a week while allowing parents to remain in the workforce. Help with groceries or bills can leave more income available for other expenses, while a home deposit can provide a pathway into a property market that might otherwise be out of reach.

Megginson said she grew up in a family that lived "pay to pay", without generational wealth to pass down.

"If you don't have generational wealth coming your way, if you're not lucky enough to be one of those 8 per cent of people who have got a house bought for them, what can you do to try and build wealth for yourself and get yourself in a better financial position?" she said.

Is financial independence changing?

Australia is also approaching a massive transfer of accumulated wealth, with previous estimates suggesting Australians aged over 60 could pass around $3.5 trillion to younger generations over two decades.

But the Booster Economy suggests some of that transfer is already happening — one grocery shop, childcare day and house deposit at a time.

Megginson believes financial pressures could even change how Australians think about independence.

While adult children remaining at home well into their 20s can sometimes be viewed as having failed to "fly the nest", she noted multigenerational living is already commonplace in many cultures.

READ MORE The taboo wealth tax debate experts say Australia can no longer ignore

"We might see a trend that is driven by finances to more embrace that style of living," she said.

"It might have some of those cultural benefits, and ... the whole 'it takes a village to raise a family' philosophy might start to flourish a little bit more."

For some Australians, that village is increasingly providing an economic safety net too — one that can look very different depending on the family you're born into.

Forrestania Resources has secured a significant ore supply stream for its Western Australian gold processing hubs, executing a deal that gives it the right to purchase and process up to two million tonnes of ore over the next two years. The company has struck two key agreements with MEGA Resources, underpinning its strategy to build a regional processing business around its Edna May and Lake Johnston facilities. Forrestania is building a regional processing hub strategy in Western Australia, with the Taipan open pit (pictured), operated by MEGA, set to provide the first ore under a new agreement. In a parallel move, Forrestania has also signed a five-year master services agreement with MEGA, establishing a preferred framework for the contractor to provide future open pit mining, drill and blast, and other mining support services. Importantly, the company says the agreement provides a mechanism to deploy services quickly without renegotiating a full contract for each project. The savvy deals slot neatly into Forrestania’s stated strategy of building a significant WA gold business by developing two complementary processing hubs at Edna May and Lake Johnston. Refurbishment of the 3.2 million tonne per annum (Mtpa) Lake Johnston mill is expected to be completed by year-end. The MEGA deal is the second major ore purchase deal the company has locked in recently, following a similar arrangement with ASX-listed First Au. That agreement provides for another two million tonnes of third-party ore from First Au’s Gimlet nearby project to feed Forrestania’s processing network. Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Sarytogan tests nail 97.7% battery-grade graphite yield Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward September 14, 2026 — 12:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sarytogan Graphite has reached a major milestone in its downstream processing ambitions, producing high-quality, battery-grade coated spherical purified graphite (CSPG) that smashed key industry specifications for use in lithium-ion batteries. Testwork on a 24-tonne bulk sample from its massive deposit in Central Kazakhstan has delivered a hefty 97.7 per cent yield, towering over the typical industry range of 50 to 60 per cent. A high yield is crucial to production economics, putting more of every tonne of mined graphite into high-value battery anode material and leaving less behind as lower-value product. Sarytogan has produced high-quality coated spherical purified graphite (pictured) from its giant deposit in Kazakhstan, exceeding key lithium-ion battery specifications. Perhaps even more significantly, the end product reached a whopping purity greater than 99.99 per cent – the coveted “four nines” mark – comfortably eclipsing the typical 99.95 per cent lithium-ion battery requirement. Sarytogan also knocked it out of the park on tap density, chalking up between 0.99 and 1.26 grams per cubic centimetre (g/cm³), a hefty improvement on its previous testwork and pushing well beyond the typical industry benchmark of about 1g/cm³. Tap density essentially measures how tightly graphite particles can pack together, with higher numbers potentially translating into more energy being squeezed into a battery. The company’s processor noted that tap densities above 1.2g/cm³ are considered “very rare” in the battery industry and are prized for their potential to enable higher energy densities in batteries.

Advertisement

‘Small sphere sizes with ultra-high tap densities are highly prized in the lithium-ion battery.’ Sarytogan Graphite managing director Sean Gregory The testwork, conducted by specialist American Energy Technologies Company in the US, produced approximately 30 kilograms of various downstream products, including ultra-high-purity fines, uncoated spherical purified graphite, and the all-important CSPG. The results are a significant step in the company’s strategy to become a vertically-integrated supplier of graphite to the burgeoning electric vehicle and energy storage markets. Sarytogan is now preparing a 5kg CSPG sample to ship to a leading European battery prototyping organisation. The material will be used to manufacture and test 5-amp-hour, large-format pouch-cell batteries, a significant scale-up from previous successful coin-cell tests and a key step in qualifying the product for potential European offtake partners. Sarytogan managing director Sean Gregory said: “These scaled-up purification, spheroidization, and coating results are an important step forward in the development of Sarytogan’s downstream graphite products. Small sphere sizes with ultra-high tap densities are highly prized in the lithium-ion battery for their associated fast-charging and high-energy-densities respectively.”

Advertisement

The company’s processing pathway, which it calls an “inverted flowsheet”, involves purifying the graphite before spheroidization. This is a clever piece of process design, as it means any graphite particles that don’t meet the size or shape specifications during spheroidization can still be sold as a premium ultra-high purity product, rather than a lower-value concentrate. All this is happening against the backdrop of Sarytogan’s colossal mineral resource, which stands at 225 million tonnes grading a remarkably high 29.2 per cent total graphitic carbon. The deposit’s scale and grade have not gone unnoticed on the world stage, with the project having been designated a Strategic Project under the European Union’s Critical Raw Materials Act, highlighting its potential as a vital future supplier to Europe. With an upstream definitive feasibility study for the mine and initial processing plant now in its final stages and due for release next quarter, the company appears to be methodically piecing together a mine-to-market plan. Meanwhile, 25 kilometres away, Sarytogan’s Baynazar copper project recently delivered the goods with a 229 metre copper hit grading 0.14 per cent copper from surface to end of hole. The impressive hit came from the Ilskan prospect and confirms the presence of a copper porphyry-style mineralised system. The company is now eagerly awaiting results from two other diamond drill holes at Ilskan. The latest downstream results provide strong proof of concept that Sarytogan’s world-class deposit can be transformed into a world-class battery product. As the company moves to test its material in commercial-style batteries, it looks as though many eyes in the EV supply chain might be watching closely. title: Historic home on one of Brisbane’s best streets sells for $17m
text:

PropertyNewsQueensland residential property Historic home on one of Brisbane’s best streets sells for $17m Sarah Webb September 14, 2026 — 11:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A landmark federation home on one of Brisbane’s best streets has clinched the nation’s top auction result of the weekend after selling for $17 million. Built in early circa 1900s, the six-bedroom estate sits on a 2,024-square-metre parcel at 1 Sutherland Avenue, Ascot, and has remained in the same family for 25 years. Four buyers registered for the Saturday auction, including two locals and two virtual bidders who phoned in from Sydney and the US. In front of a crowd at the Calile Hotel, bidding opened at $12 million with three bidders trading mostly $1 million rises. At $16.8 million, two remained and the auction paused – before selling under the hammer moments later. Ray White Collective’s Matt Lancashire marketed the home, and while unable to disclose buyer details, he said the result showed Brisbane’s defiance in the face of grim national property headlines.

Advertisement

“The campaign was amazing. We had close to 100 groups through in three weeks but when you’ve got a landmark once-in-a-generation home like this that’s why,” he said. “Houses on Sutherland Avenue just don’t come up often and it’s generally regarded as one of Brisbane’s best streets. “But this result also tells me that Brisbane’s high-end market is in good nick. “We had 10 (interested) buyers with the capacity to spend that money. The issue is there’s no stock for them to buy.” The Ascot property sits a stone’s throw from Brisbane’s second most expensive home – 32 Sutherland Avenue – which smashed the city’s price ceiling when it fetched $23 million in late 2024. In 2025, an unrenovated riverfront home at 17 Julius Street, New Farm, reset the record at $25 million.

Advertisement

For vendor Donna Scott-Young, the sale marks the end of a deeply personal chapter. Together with her family, Scott-Young bought the home for just $1.66 million in 2001 and project managed a three-year renovation in 2007. “The home is just faultless … and it has a real soul,” said Lancashire said. “You simply couldn’t replace it even if you tried.” The Ascot property was one of 159 scheduled auctions across South East Queensland over the past week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary clearance rate of 32 per cent from 115 reported results, with 16 homes withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold when calculating clearance rates.

Advertisement

In Camp Hill, a four-bedroom, two-bathroom house on a 316-square-metre parcel at 16 Grant Street sold for $2.27 million in “textbook” auction, going to a young local. A buyer’s agent opened bidding at $1.9 million, sparking a flurry of $20,000 and $10,000 rises among the four registered bidders. Despite matching every bid with a quick $1000 rise, the buyers’ agent was forced to admit defeat at $2.231 million, leaving the young man to nab the keys. “Usually buyers agents’ open quite strong to try and knock people out but this one didn’t. Their clients may have thought a deal was to be had - but good properties are still selling for fair market price,” said Shane Hicks of Place Camp Hill. “And this was a textbook circa 2025 auction … it went like clockwork and the price was right in the middle of the range we were hoping to get.”

Advertisement

Run across 17 days, Hicks said the campaign showed an emerging market trend. “We had 15 groups through the first Saturday and at the second we had just four. So that tells us the depth of buyers isn’t as deep it was, but that the serious buyers are there,” said Hicks. “And they’re getting all the listing notifications and acting quickly.” While Hicks deemed the auction a win for both the buyer and seller, he said market sentiment remained a headwind. “Buyer confidence is probably the biggest difference between the 2025 and the 2026 market,” he said.

Advertisement

“Worst case scenario we’re seeing homes sell for 5 per cent less (than the peak) … but the biggest battle right now is trying to give buyers and sellers confidence in the market.” Nearby at 43 Princess Street in Bulimba, a Cleveland couple outmuscled four other bidders to nab a “rare” four-bedroom home built by Shaun Lockyer and Black Developments – paying $4,370,000. Bought off the plan in 2021 for $3.18 million, the home sits a stone’s throw from Oxford Street on a 759-square-metre parcel and features an outdoor barbecue kitchen, a pool and a media room. Bidding opened at $3.8 million, and a sluggish, hour-long contest followed before the hammer fell.

Advertisement

“Buyers are certainly being a bit more measured with their bidding … and I think every seller is wanting a bit more for their homes but the vendors were satisfied with the result,” selling agent Scott Darwon of Ray White Bulimba said. “We’re seeing that when the properties are priced right to the market they are receiving OK inquiry and attendance at auction … but everyone is across the news and buyers are being choosy. Despite market uncertainty, Darwon said about 80 groups inspected the home thanks to its location and pedigree. “It was the sheer quality of the home. In music there was Lennon and McCartney and in Brisbane (for architectural builds) it’s Lockyer and Black,” he said. LJ Hooker chief of research Matthew Tiller said Brisbane was continuing to outperform Sydney and Melbourne, with a lack of new listings adding a bit more buoyancy.

“There are still buyers in the market and while house lending figures have fallen, they’re not zero,” he said. “There are still investors borrowing … but they’re now seeking higher yield homes. title: Stroke victim Peter would be lost without the funding that paid for his scooter. Now it’s been slashed
text:

NationalVictoriaDisability Stroke victim Peter would be lost without the funding that paid for his scooter. Now it’s been slashed Benjamin Preiss September 14, 2026 — 11:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Peter Barry was about to start an exciting new chapter in his life. He was preparing to sell his house in Colac, in Victoria’s south-west, and take a job driving heavy machinery and trucks in the West Australian mining industry. His son’s family had already moved there and lined up work for Barry. But things didn’t go to plan. A stroke changed Peter Barry’s life, but his NDIS support has reduced despite his needs. Justin McManus Just before he was due to leave in May 2019, Barry found himself lying on the floor after falling while taking a coffee cup to the kitchen sink. He dragged himself into his bedroom and stood up using the bed for support, but when he walked into the laundry, he fell again, this time cutting his head and arm on the way down.

Advertisement

“I’m laying on my back talking to myself. ‘Get up, get up, you silly bastard’,” he said. “And I couldn’t.” Barry didn’t realise that he was having a stroke. A friend found him, and he was rushed to hospital, where he learnt that at 58, he was paralysed down on his left side. Barry at home with (from left) support worker Ella Williams and support co-ordinators Prue Muvengi and Ellie McInnes. Justin McManus Though he has since regained limited movement and can now hold jars with his left hand to open them, the stroke had a profound impact on Barry’s life. He can no longer work, lost his truck licence and now drives a modified car. Despite the life-changing effect of the stroke, Barry said support from the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) enabled him to regain some independence – particularly through the provision of a motorised scooter he uses to make trips to the shops.

Advertisement

“I’d be lost without this thing,” he said. When it opened in 2013, Colac was among the first locations in Victoria to get its own NDIS office where participants and support workers could speak to staff in-person. But a recent unexplained closure for about a month has raised questions and hampered the scheme’s ability to support the community. An NDIS office in Colac closed for a month suddenly and without explanation. Shutterstock CoConnect, a Colac-based not-for-profit group which supports more than 250 people across the south-west navigate the NDIS, said the temporary closure came without warning and was an unwelcome surprise to many. “We just showed up and no one was there,” CoConnect support co-ordinator Prue Muvengi said.

Advertisement

A spokesperson for the NDIS said its Colac office was closed due to maintenance required on heating. However, other government tenants of the same building, including Centrelink, continued operating in the same space throughout the same period. Related Article Exclusive

Disability Disability provider hit by strikes as funding gap bites Victorian Liberal MP Richard Riordon said the unexplained office closure in his electorate of Polwarth was not good enough. “The unplanned closure caused great distress to many clients and client advocates who require in-person meetings and advisory,” Riordan said. He noted the closure came at the same time as transport services in the Colac area were cut for 70 residents of group homes. Though the NDIS office has since resumed operating with staff present, Muvengi said the closure had created stress and confusion for clients.

Advertisement

She said there were previous instances where the NDIS had advised her over the phone that it could not find or accept forms she had submitted online, and she had to attend the local office. The temporary closure also came on the back of Muvengi’s concerns about reductions to funding packages for Colac people living with a disability, which is complicating efforts to provide them with the support they need. Barry, pictured with support co-ordinator McInnes, says he’d be lost without his motorised scooter. Justin McManus Barry estimates his funding package has been slashed roughly in half since his stroke in 2019. While he said the first package was generous and he did not use all his funding allocation, his in-home support hours had since been reduced from two hours daily to six hours a week over three days. His funding package no longer allows for supports including a pool membership, where he could have aquatic rehabilitation.

PLC Resources has kicked off follow-up reverse-circulation (RC) drilling at its Rochefort gold prospect, part of the company’s Abbotts North gold project in Western Australia’s Murchison region, chasing what it believes could be a larger gold system lurking beyond its maiden drill pattern. An eight-hole, 2400m campaign will target northwestern and down-dip extensions of the prospect, where earlier drilling revealed strengthening gold values and a suite of geological and geochemical clues, suggesting the first holes may have clipped the edge of a bigger mineralised system. PLC Resources has started follow-up RC drilling at its Rochefort gold prospect in Western Australia’s Murchison region. The earlier five-hole, 1020m reconnaissance campaign, reported in July and representing the first modern gold drilling at the grassroots Rochefort, returned anomalous gold up to 0.4 grams per tonne (g/t) in three of five holes. The gold was hosted within highly fractionated dolerite alongside alteration, sulphidation and pathfinder geochemistry that PLC says warranted a closer look. The hotspot had already left a trail before drilling, with a 400m by 350m gold-in-soil anomaly and quartz-hematite vein rock chips grading up to 11.7g/t gold.

Advertisement

‘We’ve built a strong technical case for a larger gold system beyond our maiden drilling that all point to the northwest and at depth.’ PLC Resources executive director Simon Phillips Subsequent analysis gave PLC more indicators to follow. The company says gold values increase northwest and with depth alongside increasingly evolved dolerite, while sodic alteration interpreted as albitisation, magnesium depletion and weak but persistent sulphides, predominantly pyrrhotite, strengthen in the same direction. Multi-element work has added another pointer, withsulphur levels rising alongside elevated gold whilearsenic and antimony become relatively depleted. PLC believes the association indicates increasing proximity to a mineralising fluid pathway rather than a distal dispersion halo. The host rocks add another dash of geological spice. PLC says fractionated dolerites can make prime hunting ground for orogenic gold, pointing to Kalgoorlie’s famed Golden Mile dolerite as a geological cousin where evolved rocks often channel gold-bearing fluids before helping squeeze out their precious cargo. PLC Resources executive director Simon Phillips said: “It’s great to have the rig turning again at Rochefort. We’ve built a strong technical case for a larger gold system beyond our maiden drilling that all point the same way, to the northwest and at depth. This program is designed to directly test that target.”

Advertisement

Management expects PLC to complete the campaign in 14 days and will provide updates as drilling progresses. First assays are anticipated in four to six weeks, with results to follow as they are received and validated. The program is covered by existing environmental and heritage approvals and will be funded from existing cash reserves. In parallel, the company will continue advancing a newly interpreted regional structural corridor across its roughly 400-square-kilometre Abbotts North project. Geophysics identified a previously unmapped fold extending for more than 14km along the eastern margin of the greenstone belt that had not been recognised on existing government geological maps. The fold’s hinge intersects a deep-seated crustal structure – geological plumbing PLC regards as a first-order gold targeting feature. The company says such features can provide long-lived pathways for mineralising fluids, while their intersections can create favourable sites for those fluids to focus and deposit gold. The historic Abbotts goldfield has a strong pedigree, with records showing production of 41,000 ounces at a head grade of roughly 31g/t, principally from shallow quartz reefs. Large parts of the district have since seen little systematic modern exploration. Rochefort also sits 21km north of New Murchison Gold’s Garden Gully project in the same Abbotts Greenstone Belt. Garden Gully contains a 4.42-million-tonne resource at 2.5g/t gold for 359,300 ounces and hosts its producing Crown Prince gold mine.

PLC’s maiden drilling may not have delivered headline grades, but management believes it handed the company something potentially more useful – a geological treasure map. title: Bunnings' $19 Bluey buy sparks worrying trend despite buying limits: 'Beware'
text:
Resellers are cashing in on the popularity of a limited-edition garden item from Bunnings, with the sought-after product being flogged online for more than double its price.

The hardware store brought back its sold-out Bluey garden gnome collection last month, with a selection of characters and designs priced at $19 each.

Each time the collection lands in stores, the popular character-themed gnomes sell out quickly, with a purchase limit of four per person once again in place.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Opportunistic eBay sellers have been attempting to profit from the excitement by listing the limited-edition range online — and not for the first time.

Yahoo News Australia previously reported on the issue, with shoppers warning others to "beware of eBay resellers."

A quick search on eBay returns over 100 listings for Bunnings' Bluey garden gnome collections. In some cases, full sets of seven are priced as high as $550.

Some of the individual characters, including Bluey Tony and Hecuba, are being offloaded for between $40 and $60, roughly triple the price, despite the gnomes still being available in some stores.

A set of seven Bluey garden gnomes is listed on eBay for $550 (eBay)

Previously, a Bunnings spokesperson said they are "aware and disappointed" to see the Bluey products "being posted for resale at extremely inflated prices".

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

It did not address the new listings whenYahoo asked this week.

RELATED:

High demand for Bunnings Bluey garden gnome collection

The Bluey gnomes dropped last month and have been just as popular as in previous years, with another strong customer response.

The Bunnings collection has also sparked demand overseas, particularly in the US, with international fans expressing their desire to somehow track them down.

There are three new gnomes, such as Tony Wearing Glasses (left), and returning favourites such as Bride (right). (Bunnings)

Three new gnomes — Tony Wearing Glasses, Grandfather and Obstacle Course — have been added to the collection and have been among the strongest performers so far.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The range has been available both in-store and online at Bunnings.

A Bunnings spokesperson told Yahoo, "it's been fantastic to see the Bluey gnomes continue to be just as popular with fans this year".

"We know there are some very passionate collectors out there, and the new characters are doing really well as customers look to add to their gnome families," the spokesperson said.

"While demand has been strong, there are still Bluey gnomes available both in-store and online at Bunnings, so we'd encourage anyone keen to add a new character to their collection to jump online or check out their local store while stocks last."

Why do Aussies love viral trends?

Aussies have long been a fan of collectibles, with Woolworths Ooshies recently sending shoppers into a frenzy. In fact, they attract a similar response each and every time they drop.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Aldi's viral chopping boards, which are back in stock this week, have also caused a fuss online with Aldi loyalists desperate to snap one up.

Macquarie University consumer expert Jana Bowden told Yahoo News Australia that viral craze products have been around forever, and often, "we don't want viral craze products because we need them, we want them because everybody else has them".

She said we're "hard-wired" as humans to follow trends, and the Bunnings Bluey-themed collection is no different.

title: Shark attack leaves man in serious condition
text:
A man has been rushed to hospital with serious injuries following a shark attack at a remote beach.

Emergency services responded to Glenfield Beach, north of Geraldton in Western Australia's Midwest, shortly after 9:45am on Monday.

The man, who is in his 50s, was rushed to nearby Geraldton Health Campus under lights and sirens.

A spokesperson confirmed the man was brought to the hospital with a shark bite and was in a serious but stable condition.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The state's Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development issued an alert, saying it had received a report of a possible shark incident and was investigating further.

The public were advised to take additional caution in the Glenfield Beach area.

St John Ambulance responded to the area with two ambulances but only one was required, transporting the man as a priority one.
